title: Subtree Match
statement:
Check whether one binary tree appears inside another as a complete subtree.

Contract
- `root` and `sub` may each be null. Nodes have an integer `value` and nullable `left` and `right` children.
- Return true if some node of `root` (including `root` itself) has a subtree that is identical to `sub`: same shape, same values, and no extra descendants below the matching node.
- The empty tree is considered to appear in every tree, so a null `sub` always returns true. A null `root` with a non-null `sub` returns false. Do not modify either tree.
- Trees may be lopsided, with a height of up to 1000 nodes.

Examples
- `root = [10, 6, 12, 4, 8]` contains `sub = [6, 4, 8]`.
- `root = [10, 6, 12, 4, 8, null, null, null, 5]` does not contain `[6, 4, 8]`, because node 4 has an extra child.
- `root = [1, 1]` contains `sub = [1]`.
hints: Whether two trees are identical is one question; where in the larger tree to ask it is another.
Write a helper that tests two trees for exact equality, then try it at the root and, failing that, ask the same question about the left and right subtrees of the root.

Intended complexity: O(n * m) time for a root of n nodes and a sub of m nodes, which is O(n) when m is small and fixed, as in the performance probe. Space is the recursion depth: O(h) for tree height h, which is O(log n) for a balanced tree (the workload uses balanced trees) and O(n) for a chain.
inputSyntax: Input: two level-order trees, root then sub, separated by a semicolon, for example: [10, 6, 12, 4, 8]; [6, 4, 8]
